I've farmed these 2 mu in Quzhou for 37 years. I'm 56, only went to middle school, but I know my land better than any textbook. My wife works part-time at the textile factory in town, so it's mostly me in the fields, though she helps when the chili needs picking. We've grown chili on both mu for over 20 years now. Last year dried chili fetched about 5–6 yuan per jin, decent enough that I'm not switching crops. With only 2 mu, we can't afford big machinery or the fanciest inputs, but we know how to make it work.

This year, I'll transplant chili seedlings around May 1st, once the soil has warmed up properly. I bought improved seedlings from Old Zhang at the market — 120 yuan per mu. His seedlings always take well. I already had the small tractor come through for rotary tillage, cost me 40 yuan per mu. 

For fertilizer, here's my thinking: I put down about 80 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as base before transplanting — that's the 15-15-15 type. Then when the plants start flowering in late June, I'll spread another 20 jin of urea per mu, and another 20 jin when the fruits set in mid-July. The extension agent told me last year I could use more potassium, but the compound fertilizer has some in it, and honestly I've got to watch my cash. My wife's factory work isn't steady year-round, so I need to keep some money aside. More fertilizer might give a bit better yield, but if prices drop I'd be throwing money away. I learned that the hard way in 2019 when I bought extra and the traders only offered 4 yuan per jin.

I'll irrigate four times using the well: right after transplanting, at flowering, and twice during the hot fruiting period in July–August. Pumping costs electricity — about 50 yuan per mu for the season — so I don't water unless we've gone a week without decent rain and the plants start looking stressed.

For pesticides, I'll spray herbicide before transplanting, then insecticide two or three times for aphids and thrips, and fungicide once for that wilt disease that hit Old Wang's field last year. I buy whatever the ag supply store recommends. They know what works around here.

Labor is tight. I can handle the transplanting, weeding, fertilizing, and irrigating myself, with my wife helping on weekends. But come September and October when the red chilies need picking every few days, I'll hire three days of help at 120 yuan per day. Otherwise we'd miss the peak prices when the buyers come through the village.

I'm expecting around 2,400 jin of fresh chili per mu this year if the weather cooperates — that's about 1,200 kg per mu. Last year I got roughly the same. I dry most of it and sell to the traders. Total input cost will run me about 1,250 yuan. It's a stretch with my current cash, but my wife just got her spring bonus and we can cover it without borrowing.
